name: Helsinki-NLP OPUS-MT
maintainer: Helsinki-NLP (University of Helsinki Language Technology group)
purpose: Family of several hundred bilingual and multilingual neural MT models trained on the OPUS parallel corpora, distributed via HuggingFace with Marian/CTranslate2-compatible weights.
journalism_use_case: The default open weights for cross-border reporting: translate Russian, Ukrainian, Arabic, Turkish, Chinese or Balkan-language documents locally, with a weights licence that permits commercial publication — the specific combination most other MT options fail.
pros: CC-BY-4.0 weights (verified on the Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-ru-en card) permit commercial publication, which NLLB's CC-BY-NC and many research models do not
Hundreds of directly-trained language pairs, so you can avoid English pivoting for the pairs that matter to your reporting region
Small models — a pair is typically a few hundred MB and runs on CPU, making per-language deployment practical on field hardware
Converts cleanly to CTranslate2, so the same weights power Argos/LibreTranslate and your own batch pipelines
cons: Quality varies sharply by pair and many pairs were trained on pre-2020 OPUS data, so they are weak on current slang, OCR noise and code-switching — all characteristic of leaked material
Bilingual models mean many files to manage and a routing decision per document; language-ID errors silently produce nonsense

The Opus-MT repository itself is low-activity (pushed 2026-02-23, no releases or tags) — the models live on HuggingFace, so repository metadata understates the project's liveness but also means no version discipline
Licence must be checked per pair: CC-BY-4.0 is verified for ru-en but coverage was not confirmed across all cards
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented signal: OPUS-MT weights are the basis of Argos Translate's model packages and of many LibreTranslate deployments, which is credible evidence of practical usability. Licence was read from one HuggingFace card (opus-mt-ru-en) and generalised with explicit uncertainty.
assessment: The pragmatic choice when you need commercially usable, locally runnable MT for a specific language pair. Build your pipeline to record which model ID and revision translated each document, because quality differences between pairs are large enough to affect editorial confidence in a quoted passage. Where quality is insufficient and the material is not commercially published, NLLB may be better — but check that distinction deliberately rather than letting a model choice create a licence problem.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: Helsinki-NLP/Opus-MT archived=false, pushed_at 2026-02-23, no releases, no tags, 876 stars, 57 open issues. The models are maintained on HuggingFace rather than through repository releases, so repo quiescence understates activity; however, there is no visible release cadence to evidence active maintenance. Classified stable-low: the model family is functionally complete and widely consumed.
model_or_data_licence: CC-BY-4.0 verified on the HuggingFace card for Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-ru-en; coverage varies, check each pair.
licence_restrictions: CC-BY-4.0 requires attribution — include the model card citation in your methodology note. No non-commercial restriction on the verified pair.
costs: No fee. CPU inference, a few hundred MB per pair. No paid dependencies.
privacy: Local inference after download; nothing leaves the machine. Weights can be staged offline.
alternatives: Argos Translate for a packaged offline library over the same lineage
NLLB-200 or MADLAD-400 via CTranslate2 for better low-resource coverage — but verify the licence, NLLB is CC-BY-NC
Commercial MT APIs only for non-sensitive public material

name: Hyperaudio Lite
purpose: Lightweight dependency-free JavaScript library that binds a timed transcript to an audio or video element, giving click-to-seek, karaoke-style highlighting and in-transcript search.
journalism_use_case: Publishing the evidence alongside the story: an embeddable, searchable transcript of an interview or council hearing where a reader can click any sentence and hear it in the original recording. That turns 'we have a recording' into verifiable published evidence and pre-empts quote-distortion accusations.
pros: Solves the last-mile publishing problem that transcription tools ignore — the reader-facing artefact, not the transcript file
No dependencies and entirely client-side, so it adds no backend, no tracking and no third-party scripts to a story page
MIT and tiny, so a newsroom front-end developer can adapt it in an afternoon
Maintained by the team that has worked on this specific problem for years, with a current release (v2.6.6, 2026-09-21)
cons: Presentation layer only: the timed transcript must be produced elsewhere (WhisperX, noScribe) and converted to the expected HTML/WebVTT shape
Small niche project (183 stars, 42 open issues) — the open-issue-to-star ratio is high, suggesting limited maintainer bandwidth relative to requests
Accessibility, styling and mobile behaviour are largely left to the implementer, so a polished result takes design work
Whatever you publish is public by design, so redaction decisions must be final before the transcript is embedded — there is no partial-disclosure mechanism
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Hyperaudio's lineage in media/journalism prototyping is long-standing and documented by the project, but I verified no specific newsroom deployment; treat adoption as plausible rather than evidenced.
assessment: A small, high-leverage addition if your newsroom publishes audio-based investigations. For your profile the integration is trivial relative to the editorial payoff, and the privacy profile is clean — no third-party player, no tracking. The one discipline it demands is that the transcript be redaction-final, since publishing a clickable transcript exposes every word of the recording you ship with it.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-30, latest release v2.6.6 (2026-09-21), 183 stars, 42 open issues. Regular small releases from a small team; functionally complete library with modest change velocity.
costs: No fee, no infrastructure beyond your existing web hosting. Cost is front-end developer time for styling and accessibility.
privacy: Entirely client-side with no network calls of its own, so it introduces no tracking into a story page — notably better than embedding a third-party player. The published transcript and media are public by definition.
alternatives: Subtitle Edit to produce and verify the timed file first
Custom WebVTT plus a standard HTML5 player if you need less than Hyperaudio offers
oTranscribe for transcription-time workflows rather than publishing

name: ICIJ Datashare
purpose: Self-hosted document-analysis platform that extracts text and entities from a document collection and gives journalists a search, tagging and review interface, available as a desktop application or a multi-user server deployment.
journalism_use_case: The reference end-to-end newsroom stack for a leaked document set: one journalist can run it as a desktop app over 50,000 files, or a cross-border team can run it in server mode and share tags and saved searches across an investigation — the architecture ICIJ built for its own cross-border projects.
pros: Built by the organisation that runs the largest cross-border leak investigations, so the workflow assumptions (tagging, batch search, team sharing) match how reporting actually happens
Desktop mode is the standout feature: a journalist with no infrastructure gets OCR plus NER plus search on their own laptop, with the documents never leaving it
Explicitly designed so no external cloud services are required — the README states sensitive material stays under your control, which is the correct architecture for source protection
Very active: pushed 2026-11-17 with release 21.24.2 on 2026-11-16, and multiple NER backends (CoreNLP, Ixa Pipes, MITIE) bundled
cons: Server mode needs real infrastructure — Elasticsearch, PostgreSQL, Redis — and the operational capacity to run them; this is where small newsrooms stall
Entity types are limited to person/organisation/location, so it indexes and surfaces rather than resolving entities; cross-document identity work needs nomenklatura or manual effort
AGPL-3.0 obligations apply if you modify it and host it for others, which constrains building a customised newsroom service on top
Elasticsearch dependency carries the Elastic licensing question that Solr/OpenSearch avoid — relevant if you redistribute a bundled deployment
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The strongest documented signal is institutional: ICIJ builds and uses Datashare for its own investigations, and the release cadence (21.24.x in November 2026) reflects a tool under continuous internal use. 783 stars, 76 open issues.
assessment: For a small newsroom I would recommend Datashare desktop over almost anything else in this pillar — it is the shortest path from 'we received a dump' to 'reporters are searching it' without an engineer. In server mode the choice between Datashare and OpenAleph is close: Datashare has the better reporter UI and institutional backing; OpenAleph has the stronger entity model and cross-referencing against sanctions and registry data. If your investigations are document-centric, choose Datashare; if they are entity-centric, choose OpenAleph.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 21.24.2 (2026-11-16), 783 stars, 76 open issues. Daily-scale commits, releases within the week, and an institutional owner that depends on the tool operationally — the strongest form of maintenance evidence available.
model_or_data_licence: n/a for the platform; bundled NER models carry their own terms and were not individually verified.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0 network copyleft: modifying Datashare and offering it over a network to third parties obliges you to publish your modified source. Running it unmodified for your own newsroom is unaffected.
costs: No software fee. Desktop mode: zero infrastructure. Server mode estimate: an Elasticsearch node with 8-16GB RAM, PostgreSQL, Redis and worker capacity — realistically one well-provisioned VM for a few hundred thousand documents, scaling with OCR load. Assumptions: self-hosted, no managed Elasticsearch. Operating effort is the dominant cost in server mode.
privacy: Designed for local custody: no third-party services are required, documents remain on your hardware, and desktop mode keeps everything on one machine. Residual risks: Elasticsearch must not be exposed, and in server mode the index becomes a high-value target that needs encryption at rest and strict access control.
alternatives: OpenAleph where entity cross-referencing against sanctions and registries is the priority
Uwazi for public-facing document collections
Paperless-ngx for a small internal archive with far lower operational cost

name: ICIJ extract
purpose: JVM command-line tool that walks a file tree or archive, extracts text and metadata via Apache Tika with parallel workers and Redis-backed queueing, OCRs images, and writes results to Solr or Elasticsearch.
journalism_use_case: Purpose-built for this domain: the lineage ICIJ used to process multi-terabyte leaks, designed to chew through millions of mixed files, OCR the scanned ones at scale, and feed a search index — the unglamorous stage where most home-grown leak pipelines fall over.
pros: Engineered for the specific failure modes of real leaks — resumable queues, parallel workers, per-file error isolation so one corrupt PDF does not kill a run
Direct Solr/Elasticsearch output means it slots into an index-first architecture without intermediate storage
MIT licensed and used by ICIJ at terabyte scale: the most relevant provenance any tool in this subcategory can have
Current activity (pushed 2026-11-13, tag 9.23.0) with a very clean issue tracker (4 open)
cons: No tagged GitHub releases (only tags), no UI, and documentation written for operators who already understand the architecture — the learning curve is real
Small user base outside ICIJ, so community answers to operational problems are scarce
The OCR step is only as good as Tesseract, which caps accuracy on degraded scans regardless of throughput
JVM plus Redis plus a search index is three moving parts before you have indexed a single document
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The institutional signal is the point: ICIJ maintains and uses it, and the 4 open issues against 257 stars indicate a small but attended project. No third-party newsroom deployment verified.
assessment: Choose extract when you are deliberately building an index-first architecture at a scale where Datashare's bundled ingest is the bottleneck. For most of your likely work, Datashare or OpenAleph's ingest-file already wraps this capability with a UI, and standing up extract separately is only justified by scale or by a bespoke index schema. Its credibility is high; its audience is narrow.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-13, latest tag 9.23.0, no release objects, 257 stars, 4 open issues. Recent commits and a 9.x tag line, maintained by an organisation that runs it in production. The absence of release objects is a hygiene gap, not an activity signal.
licence_restrictions: None material; note it bundles Tika, whose third-party notices must be reproduced on redistribution.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure: JVM workers scaled to CPU count, Redis, plus the downstream index. OCR dominates compute on scanned corpora — budget CPU-hours roughly proportional to page count. Estimate; assumes self-hosted.
privacy: Fully self-hosted and designed for controlled leak handling; no external calls in the extraction path.
alternatives: openaleph/ingest-file for the same stage inside an OpenAleph deployment
Apache Tika server plus your own queue if you want Python-native orchestration
Datashare, which bundles this capability behind a UI

name: ingest-file (OpenAleph fork)
maintainer: OpenAleph / DARC (maintained fork of the archived alephdata/ingest-file)
purpose: Worker service that ingests heterogeneous files — documents, mailboxes, archives, images, spreadsheets — converts and OCRs them, and emits FollowTheMoney entities for indexing by OpenAleph.
journalism_use_case: The extraction and OCR stage of an entity-centric leak pipeline: it turns a directory of mixed attachments, PST mailboxes and scans into structured FtM records, so the archive can be cross-referenced against sanctions lists and registries rather than merely searched.
pros: Emits FollowTheMoney entities rather than plain text, which is what enables cross-dataset linking downstream — a materially different output from Tika-only pipelines
Maintained fork of an archived upstream, with releases tracking OpenAleph (5.4.0, 2026-11-12), so the lineage problem is solved rather than inherited
Handles mailbox and archive formats that defeat most Python-first ingest tools, via Tika and LibreOffice-family converters
Containerised worker model scales horizontally and isolates parsing of untrusted files
cons: Very small contributor base (15 stars, 8 open issues) — it exists to serve OpenAleph and is not a general-purpose library with a community behind it
AGPL-3.0 copyleft affects redistribution of modified services, which matters if you build a product around the ingest stage
OCR throughput is the usual bottleneck on scanned corpora and the fork does not change that ceiling
Effectively coupled to OpenAleph: using it standalone means adopting the FtM model and writing your own consumer
feedback: No user reports collected. The relevant documented finding is lineage, verified this session: the upstream alephdata/ingest-file is archived while this fork releases in step with OpenAleph 5.4.0 (2026-11-12) — concrete evidence that the maintained path has moved.
assessment: Only adopt it as part of an OpenAleph deployment; as a standalone ingest library ICIJ extract or plain Tika is a better fit. Its catalogue value is that it answers the question 'is Aleph's ingest stack dead?' — the upstream is, this fork is not. For your profile that distinction is the actionable fact.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release 5.4.0 (2026-11-12), 15 stars, 8 open issues. Releases are version-locked to OpenAleph, which is itself actively released; maintenance is institutional (DARC) rather than community-driven.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: modified network-service redistribution triggers source-release obligations. Internal use is unaffected.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure: containerised workers sized to OCR load, plus the OpenAleph stack it feeds. Estimate only.
privacy: Local processing in worker containers; no external calls required. Container isolation is a genuine security benefit when parsing untrusted files.
alternatives: ICIJ extract for a standalone Solr-targeted pipeline
Apache Tika server for format extraction without the FtM layer
Docling where layout fidelity matters more than entity emission

name: Kraken
purpose: Trainable OCR and handwritten-text-recognition engine with baseline segmentation, support for right-to-left and bidirectional scripts, and ALTO/PAGE XML output.
journalism_use_case: The practical open engine for archival investigations — handwritten registers, ledgers, colonial-era records, Arabic and Hebrew manuscripts — where a model fine-tuned on a few hundred transcribed lines of the specific hand turns an unreadable archive into searchable text.
pros: Fine-tuning on a small ground-truth set is the capability that matters: generic OCR fails on a specific hand, and Kraken is designed for exactly that adaptation
First-class support for right-to-left and bidirectional scripts, a genuine gap in Tesseract's practical quality
Outputs ALTO and PAGE XML, so transcriptions feed archival search systems and remain usable long term
Current releases (7.1, 2026-08-05) and a clean tracker (29 open issues) for a specialist tool
cons: Steep learning curve: segmentation models, recognition models and ground-truth formats are all concepts you must learn before results improve
Accuracy on an unseen hand usually requires fine-tuning with manually transcribed lines — the human cost is the real cost, often days of transcription
Public models are published on Zenodo with per-model terms that vary and were not individually verified, so licence diligence is per model
CLI-only; a team workflow requires eScriptorium on top, which is a much larger deployment
feedback: No user reports collected. Documented context: Kraken is the recognition engine behind eScriptorium and the standard choice in digital-humanities HTR — strong adjacent-field adoption evidence, no verified journalism deployment.
assessment: Use it when the material is handwritten or in a non-Latin historical script and nothing else works; otherwise Tesseract, Surya or PaddleOCR will cost you far less. For your profile the deciding question is whether you have the human capacity to produce ground truth — without that, Kraken's main advantage is unavailable and you are better off with a general OCR engine plus manual reading.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-10, latest release 7.1 (2026-08-05), latest tag 7.1.1, 1,107 stars, 29 open issues. Major-version releases on a regular cadence from a single academic maintainer; low issue count indicates attention. Single-maintainer bus factor is the risk, not activity.
model_or_data_licence: Varies by model — public models are published on Zenodo with per-model terms; not individually verified in this survey.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive. Verify the licence of each Zenodo-published model before commercial use; some academic models carry non-commercial or attribution conditions.
costs: No fee. A GPU materially accelerates training and inference. The dominant cost is human transcription to build ground truth — budget days of specialist labour per hand. Estimate.
privacy: Local; optional model fetch from Zenodo is the only network event. Suitable for sensitive archives on isolated hardware.
alternatives: eScriptorium for a collaborative team interface over the same engine
Transkribus as a hosted alternative with published pricing — but it moves material to a third party
Surya or PaddleOCR for printed or modern typeset material

name: LibreTranslate
purpose: Self-hostable translation API and web UI built on Argos Translate, with a REST interface, language auto-detection, API-key management and rate limiting.
journalism_use_case: A newsroom-run translation endpoint so no document text leaves the organisation: point OpenAleph, Datashare or your own ingest pipeline at it for bulk gisting of foreign-language material, and give reporters a browser UI that looks like the cloud services they would otherwise paste leaked text into.
pros: Replaces the behaviour you most need to stop — pasting sensitive text into a public translation site — with something that looks the same but stays inside the perimeter
REST API with rate limiting and keys makes it a shared newsroom service rather than a personal tool
Dockerised and genuinely easy to deploy; one of the lower-effort self-hosting jobs in this catalogue
Large community (17,778 stars) and current releases (v1.9.6, 2026-05-26)
cons: Translation quality is well below commercial MT on low-resource pairs because it inherits Argos/OPUS models — adequate for triage, not for publication

AGPL-3.0 network copyleft applies if you expose a modified instance to users, which is exactly the deployment shape most newsrooms want — unmodified deployment is fine, but customising the UI creates an obligation
No translation memory, glossary or human-review workflow, so terminology consistency across an investigation is unmanaged
The public libretranslate.com API is the same software but a third party — the convenience path is the insecure one, and staff will find it
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented signals: 17,778 stars and 136 open issues indicate wide adoption with active triage; the project documents both self-hosted and hosted (paid) options, so the hosted-versus-self-hosted distinction is explicit rather than hidden.
assessment: I would deploy this for any newsroom handling foreign-language material — the privacy argument is decisive and the deployment cost is low. Two concrete controls: block libretranslate.com at the network level so staff use your instance, and keep your deployment unmodified (configuration, not code changes) to avoid the AGPL publication obligation. Accept that output is triage-grade and route anything quotable to a human translator.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release v1.9.6 (2026-05-26), 17,778 stars, 136 open issues. Current commits, periodic releases, large community. Classified active on the combination rather than push recency alone.
model_or_data_licence: Inherits Argos Translate model packages (largely open, derived from OPUS/OPUS-MT data); verify per language pair.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: if you modify LibreTranslate and provide it over a network, you must offer your modified source to users. Running it unmodified for internal use carries no obligation.
costs: No software fee for self-hosting. Infrastructure estimate: one CPU VM with 4-8GB RAM serves a small newsroom; each language pair adds a few hundred MB of models. The hosted libretranslate.com service has paid API tiers whose current prices were NOT verified in this survey. Assumptions: self-hosted Docker, CPU-only.
privacy: Fully local when self-hosted — the core reason to run it. The counterpart risk is explicit: the public API sends text to a third party and must be avoided for leak material. Model downloads occur on first run.
alternatives: Argos Translate directly for scripted batch work without a service
Helsinki-NLP OPUS-MT via CTranslate2 for better per-pair control
A commercial MT API only for already-public material

name: Marker
purpose: Converts PDFs, Office files and images to Markdown, JSON or HTML using the Surya model family for layout, reading order, table structure and OCR, with optional LLM-assisted accuracy enhancement.
journalism_use_case: Workhorse for turning a heterogeneous leak — mixed PDFs, Office files, scans — into clean Markdown that is searchable, diffable and quotable, with page-level traceability back to the original. In practice the best-quality local conversion available for messy real-world documents.
pros: Conversion quality on messy multi-column and tabular documents is at or near the top of the open field, which directly reduces the downstream reading burden on reporters
Apache-2.0 code, very active (v2.2.0, 2026-11-12), 40,946 stars — exceptional momentum and responsiveness (82 open issues)
Handles the full pipeline (layout, reading order, tables, OCR) rather than requiring you to assemble four components
Page-level provenance in the output makes extracted passages citable back to the source document
cons: The weights are NOT open source: the README labels them OpenRAIL-M and links to datalab.to/pricing, where commercial use above $5M in revenue OR funding (for Marker and Surya) requires a paid licence — verified on the vendor page 2026-11-16
The accuracy-boosting LLM mode sends page content to an external provider unless pointed at a self-hosted model — an exfiltration path that must be explicitly closed for source material
GPU effectively required for useful throughput on large corpora; CPU conversion of a big dump is impractical
Two-tier licensing means your compliance position depends on your organisation's revenue and funding, which can change mid-project
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented, checkable facts: 40.9k stars with 82 open issues (strong adoption and triage); and the vendor's own pricing page stating the commercial threshold verbatim — 'free for commercial use if your company is under the threshold on both revenue and funding: $2M for Chandra and $5M for Marker and Surya' (verified 2026-11-16, recorded in sources/recovered/cat/pricing.tsv).
assessment: Technically my first choice for conversion quality, but the weights licence makes it a conditional recommendation. For a small independent newsroom or an exile outlet under the thresholds, adopt it and document the revenue/funding position in writing. For a larger publisher, or where you cannot be certain of funding levels across a consortium, Docling is the safer default even at some quality cost. Disable the LLM enhancement mode by configuration for any sensitive corpus.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release v2.2.0 (2026-11-12), 40,946 stars, 82 open issues. Frequent releases, commercially backed by Datalab, low issue backlog relative to size.
model_or_data_licence: OpenRAIL-M for the Surya/Datalab weights (README 'Model License: OpenRAIL-M' linking to datalab.to/pricing). NOT OSI-approved. Commercial use above $5M revenue OR funding requires a paid licence.
licence_restrictions: Revenue/funding threshold on the weights is the material restriction; OpenRAIL-M also imposes use-based behavioural restrictions that flow downstream on redistribution. Code licence does not cure the weights licence.
costs: Code free. Weights free below the threshold; above it, a commercial licence is required at a price not publicly listed (quote required). Datalab's hosted API: Free $0 pay-as-you-go with a $20/$10 monthly allowance, Team $400/month, Enterprise custom (vendor page, verified 2026-11-16, USD). Self-hosted infrastructure: one GPU host; if the LLM mode is used against a third-party API, add those token costs (not priced here).
privacy: Local by default. Two explicit external paths: first-run weight download, and the optional LLM-enhancement mode which transmits page content to whatever endpoint is configured. The hosted Datalab API is a third-party custody decision and is inappropriate for unpublished source material.
alternatives: Docling — recommended where the weights licence is unacceptable or revenue exceeds the threshold
Surya directly for the underlying OCR/layout models without Marker's orchestration
PaddleOCR / PP-StructureV3 for CJK and Arabic-heavy corpora
blockers: Weights are OpenRAIL-M with a $5M revenue-or-funding commercial threshold — a licence decision, not a technical one

name: Montreal Forced Aligner
purpose: Kaldi-based forced aligner that time-aligns a known transcript to an audio recording at word and phone level, with pretrained acoustic models and pronunciation dictionaries for many languages.
journalism_use_case: Authenticating or precisely timestamping a known transcript against a recording — essential when you must demonstrate that a specific phrase occurs at a specific moment in leaked audio, or when verifying that a circulating 'transcript' of a speech matches the actual recording.
pros: Produces phone-level timing that no ASR system gives you, which is what makes forensic-grade claims about audio possible
Pretrained models and dictionaries for a wide range of languages, so it is not English-only like much speech tooling
Mature, academically grounded and actively released (v3.4.4, 2026-11-16) — unusual longevity for a research tool
Deterministic: given the same inputs it produces the same alignment, which is what an evidentiary workflow needs
cons: Aligns, does not recognise — you must supply a correct transcript, so it complements rather than replaces transcription
Requires a pronunciation dictionary for the language, and out-of-dictionary proper names (ubiquitous in investigations) degrade alignment precisely where it matters
Conda-only installation plus a PostgreSQL corpus database is an awkward and heavy dependency chain
292 open issues against 1,918 stars — the highest backlog ratio in this subcategory, suggesting support demand exceeds capacity
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented signals: active releases through 2026-11-16 alongside a 292-issue backlog — a maintained project with a support deficit. Strong adoption in phonetics/linguistics research; no journalism deployment verified.
assessment: A specialist instrument: adopt it only when an audio-authentication or precise-timestamping question is actually on the table, in which case nothing else does the job. For your profile I would install it on demand rather than keep it in the standard stack, and I would pre-build a custom pronunciation dictionary for the proper names central to the investigation — that single step is what determines whether the alignment is usable.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v3.4.4 published the same day (2026-11-16), 1,918 stars, 292 open issues. Same-day push and release demonstrates active maintenance; the large backlog is a responsiveness limitation rather than evidence of decline.
model_or_data_licence: Pretrained acoustic models and dictionaries are distributed separately per language — verify each; some derive from corpora with their own terms.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive. Per-language model and dictionary terms need checking before commercial use.
costs: No fee. Costs are a conda environment, a PostgreSQL instance and CPU time proportional to audio hours; plus specialist time to build dictionaries. Estimate.
privacy: Fully local; model and dictionary downloads from the project index are the only network events. Suitable for sensitive audio on isolated hardware.
alternatives: WhisperX, whose wav2vec2 alignment gives word-level timing with far less setup and is sufficient for most quote-verification needs
Subtitle Edit for manual waveform-based verification by a non-engineer
Praat for forensic phonetic analysis by a specialist

name: nomenklatura
purpose: Entity-resolution and deduplication toolkit for FollowTheMoney data: candidate generation, scoring algorithms, an interactive adjudication loop, and a resolver file recording every merge decision.
journalism_use_case: The deduplication engine behind OpenSanctions: merge the same oligarch or company across sanctions lists, leaks and corporate registries while keeping an auditable record of every merge a human approved — so a later challenge to 'how do you know these are the same person' has a documented answer.
pros: The resolver file is the standout feature: entity-resolution decisions become a version-controlled artefact rather than a black box, which is exactly what investigative accountability requires
Battle-tested in production on OpenSanctions' own cross-source dataset, which is one of the larger continuously-resolved entity datasets in existence
Interactive adjudication keeps a human in the loop on borderline merges rather than silently guessing
Current and frequently released (4.17.3, 2026-10-21) under MIT
cons: Only speaks FollowTheMoney, so arbitrary CSVs must first be mapped into the ontology — a non-trivial modelling step that is the real adoption cost
Documentation assumes familiarity with the OpenSanctions pipeline; there is no standalone tutorial for a newsroom coming in cold
Resolver files become long-lived artefacts that must be managed and migrated, and a corrupted or lost resolver loses your merge history
Enrichment connectors can query external APIs (OpenCorporates, Wikidata) — off by default, but a configuration mistake would send entity names to a third party
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The production signal is verifiable from the OpenSanctions codebase: nomenklatura is the resolution layer of a publicly operated dataset, released on a regular cadence (273 stars, 19 open issues).
assessment: If you adopt FollowTheMoney, adopt nomenklatura with it — the pairing is what gives you auditable cross-dataset identity. If you are not using FtM, Splink is the better general-purpose choice and nomenklatura's mapping overhead is not worth it. For your profile the resolver-as-artefact design is the strongest argument: it converts a methodological weakness of investigative data work into something you can show an editor or a lawyer.

model_or_data_licence: n/a for the code. Note that OpenSanctions DATA is CC-BY-NC-4.0 and separately licensed — see the OpenSanctions entry.
licence_restrictions: Code unrestricted. The restriction appears if you resolve against OpenSanctions data commercially — that is a data-licence question, not a code one.
costs: No fee. Optional Elasticsearch/OpenSearch and Redis for candidate generation at scale; CPU-bound otherwise. The dominant cost is human adjudication time on borderline pairs. Estimate.
privacy: Local by default. Enrichment connectors to OpenCorporates or Wikidata must be explicitly configured and would disclose the names you are resolving — review before enabling on a confidential list.
alternatives: Splink for general-purpose probabilistic linkage without the FtM requirement
rigour for the normalisation stage that precedes resolution
dedupe for small analyst-driven jobs, with the maintenance caveat noted in its entry
